data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A small research team should build a custom experiment tracker only when the experimental design requires the tracker to function as an active controller in a closed-loop system (e.g., active learning or Bayesian optimization), where the latency and schema rigidity of existing tools would break the causal chain of the experiment; otherwise, they must adopt an existing tool to avoid the 'integration tax' and 'migration cliff'.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The team lacks the engineering bandwidth to maintain a custom state machine without halting research progress.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The active learning loop can be simulated via external scripts that interface with an existing tracker's API without requiring the tracker itself to be the controller.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The experimental schema is stable enough that a rigid existing tool does not force data distortion.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Causal Control Boundary: The decision boundary is defined by whether the tracker must write back to the experimental apparatus in real-time. If the tracker is purely observational (read-only log), existing tools maximize bandwidth. If the tracker is actuatory (read-write control loop), custom software is required to maintain the causal mechanism's integrity, as off-the-shelf tools abstract away the specific state-transition logic needed for novel active learning loops.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
